questions.q: What is the programme mainly about?
options: The life and work of Albert Einstein
What algorithms are and how they help us
How to cook pancakes using a simple recipe
Why internet dating has become so popular
questions.why: Neil says algorithms are all around us, and 'they're the topic of this programme'.

questions.q: Why does Neil mention credit cards, internet dating and traffic lights?
options: To show that computers often make mistakes
To explain how banks make their money
To show how modern life has become stressful
They're examples of things that use algorithms
questions.why: He says they all involve computers, and they all use algorithms.

questions.q: According to Neil, what is a simple way to think of algorithms?
options: Like recipes
Like maps
Like games
Like letters
questions.why: He says, 'A simple way to think of algorithms is as recipes.'

options: Since the first computers
Since Einstein's time
Since Babylonian times
Only for the last few decades
questions.why: Sam says they've been around since Babylonian times, around 4,000 years ago.

questions.q: Why can algorithms be controversial today?
options: They make computers work too slowly
Some have been accused of racial prejudice
They are too expensive for most companies
They are only understood by mathematicians
questions.why: Neil says some algorithms used in internet search engines have been accused of racial prejudice.

questions.q: What is Professor Ramesh Srinivasan's view of algorithms?
options: They are dangerous and should be controlled
They are a mystery that nobody understands
They will soon replace human workers
They're simply sets of repeated instructions
questions.why: He says they're not the bogyman or mysterious – just a repeated set of instructions to solve a problem.

questions.q: What does the apple example show about algorithms?
options: Computers are better at picking fruit than people
Big apples are always harder to sort
They find the quickest, most efficient method
Every tree needs its own special algorithm
questions.why: Sorting apples tree by tree is easier, and Neil says algorithms find the most efficient way to get things done.

questions.q: What example does Professor Ian Stewart give?
options: A computer sorting emails by date
A shop sorting all its customers by age
A phone finding the fastest route home
A pizza company planning its deliveries
questions.why: He describes a computer sorting 500 emails by date 'in a flash', which would take ages by hand.
